In this production, which feels right all the way through, it is as if Frankie and Johnny can’t achieve intimacy on their own but need an external vocabulary.
Together they turn their unlikely chemistry into something electric, and in doing so reanimate material that may otherwise have felt near its expiration date.
They connect, and they draw us in.

Shannon and McDonald — playing the only two characters onstage — as well as Arbus seem to be clearly aware of the minefields to be avoided.
That they’ve survived their fears, our worries and the demands of two very different eras is as miraculous today as it was in 1987.

In the emotional and beautifully performed revival of Terrence McNally’s 1987 'Frankie and Johnny in the Claire de Lune' at the Broadhurst Theatre, the ecstasy turns out to be fleeting, the couple completely at odds over where this relationship is going.
Their superb work proves that Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune offers both timeless themes and eternal catnip to talented performers.
McDonald and Shannon are both wonderful actors, but they seem to be performing in different plays.
By contrast, while McDonald and Shannon are both fun to watch, their turbulent chemistry alone doesn’t sustain McNally’s somewhat overstretched play.

Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune is as open and honest about the human heart as anything you are likely to encounter on a Broadway stage, and the music that gives the play its title is reflected in the duet of the performances.

As drawn by the playwright Terrence McNally, Frankie and Johnny are two ordinary, working class characters. However, with Audra McDonald and Michael Shannon portraying the couple, we’re granted more than perfect bodies and movie star looks to appreciate, not to mention their outstanding acting.
The production is anchored in two of the best performances currently on Broadway.
McNally's two-character play, set during those early morning "what now?" hours immediately after a pair that only casually knows each other has had sex for the first time, is wonderful.
McDonald and Shannon slip into their characters' battered souls, finding new shadings and tiny revelations that make them seem freshly conceived.
Gorgeously acted, this sophisticated two-hander from 1987 offers some surprisingly prescient insights about love in the age of Tinder.
Mismatched characters, yes; played here by the mismatched but equally brilliant Audra McDonald and Michael Shannon, Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune positively soars.
And what makes “Frankie + Johnny” still work so well is that the pair’s ability to finally open up to each other, in every sense of the word, is really quite beautiful
McNally’s hopeful and heartfelt dramedy still carries a message for audiences who have grown perhaps even more jaded about love than those of three decades ago.

That being said, the play itself (which runs roughly 2½ hours and is confined to Frankie’s studio apartment) is very thin.

My major qualm with this production, under the attentive direction of Arin Arbus, is that the play set in front of us is arguably less about Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune than it is about Audra and Michael in the spotlight.
Frankie and Johnny may be catnip for actors, but I question the decision to revive this play.
For all the virtuosity on display, I’m not sure that we ever truly believe the characters, believe that these people are as lonely, and as needy, as the script requires them to be.
I’ve never met these “working-class” people in my life.

cn.t: McDonald and Shannon deliver superb performances in this McNally revival, though critics are divided on whether the 1987 play's sexual politics have aged well. Most praise the acting chemistry, but some find the dynamic dated and problematic.

sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name Center Orchestra rows D-K as the house sweet spot; Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang does not begin cutting the stage picture until row K, so D-K sits entirely in front of the overhang line while still clearing the shallow front-row rake. SeatPlan editors specifically advise skipping rows A-C because the Broadhurst stage pushes action to the sides that front-row patrons miss.

Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang begins at row K and, per Headout and SeatPlan, 'visibly cuts into the top of the stage by row R' - specifically blocking projections and anything that plays high. The rake in these rear orchestra rows is also called out as shallow, compounding the loss of vertical stage picture.

SeatPlan specifically flags the Broadhurst's Left and Right Boxes as overhanging far-aisle orchestra seats around rows D-F, cutting off the corresponding side of the stage, and the three elevated boxes themselves 'sit at quite sharp angles' with unfixed chairs. Headout adds that double-digit seats near the aisle get only partial views of the stage.

Multiple sources (Headout, SeatPlan, NewYorkTheatreGuide) call Center Mezzanine rows A-B the second-best location in the house. The Broadhurst's front mezzanine ledge has no railing, so shorter patrons aren't blocked - a Broadhurst-specific quirk noted by both SeatPlan and Headout. Because there is no balcony above, front-mezz rows have zero overhang.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine rows C-F the value pick - 'enough rake to see over the top of heads' at sub-premium pricing - and because Broadhurst has no balcony above, the rear mezzanine is not overhung itself. The back four rows are slightly shorter with a decent rake, and a Tripadvisor reviewer (Apr 2024) reported a 'crystal clear view' from the last row of the mezzanine.
